extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners; PR managers and counselors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing, retaining, collaborating with, and evaluating outside public relations firms and on intraorganizational coordination (PR with IT, HR, CPO, etc.). Covers pitch requirements, billing, advantages/disadvantages of outside counsel, standards and accreditation, and operational cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination of public relations and human resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations may combine oversight of public relations and human resources (example: Hershey named a senior VP and 'chief people officer' to oversee both PR and HR). Absent such coordination, organizations create new units to conceive and implement internal and external communication strategy to support restructuring and cultural change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate PR and HR when managing restructuring or culture change so internal and external messaging align; consider creating a joint unit or common leadership to avoid siloed communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of IT into public relations strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Information technology departments often set up and manage email, messaging, websites, Internet conferencing, and social media separate from public relations, which can mean new technology platforms are not part of the larger public relations strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure IT initiatives are integrated with PR strategy to avoid fragmented platforms and inconsistent messaging; involve PR in platform choice and messaging design rather than leaving it solely to IT.

rubrics_metrics.name: One voice approach in public statements and branding
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'one voice' approach ensures consistency in public statements, branding, and other public relations program components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate across departments (PR, IT, marketing, HR, legal) to maintain consistent public messaging and branding across channels and platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR-led social media strategy (not tech-only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology personnel may focus on 'providing a platform' rather than 'delivering a solution' and therefore fail to develop adequate social media initiatives; PR staff bring understanding of stakeholder needs, concerns, and intended outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have public relations lead social media strategy and message development while IT supports platform delivery; avoid handing social media exclusively to tech staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness and crisis agility of PR
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations practitioners must be able to respond immediately and nimbly in day-to-day media relations and crisis communication; time is critical when the media call or crises threaten organizational survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize rapid PR decision-making and clear escalation paths during crises; do not rely on slower-paced departments for time-sensitive media responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for PR technical competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Few public relations staff have the technical background and skill necessary to understand and develop rapidly evolving communication technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in PR staff training or bring in specialists to bridge technical gaps so PR can harness new technologies effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdepartmental collaboration (PR with IT and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations collaborates with other departments to help avoid or solve problems; IT likewise works with other departments. Seldom can either PR or IT solve problems on its own because both are staff functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster structured collaboration processes (joint planning, shared KPIs, cross-functional teams) between PR, IT, HR, marketing, legal, finance, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration with business intelligence/Chief Performance Officer (CPO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations should work closely with the CPO (business intelligence unit) to identify stakeholders, determine relationship indicators, and communicate the KPIs continuously so all know when efforts are working or failing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage PR in KPI selection, stakeholder mapping, and ongoing communication of performance metrics; integrate PR into business intelligence discussions at senior-management tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and organizational buy-in for Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)
rubrics_metrics.description: KPIs serve to benchmark and track progress on process and outcome indicators; all departments must be on board with the KPIs used to guide efforts, document progress, and make strategic course corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop KPIs collaboratively, ensure relevant departments (HR, PR, operations) understand and commit to them, and communicate KPI status continuously to stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and accreditation: PRCA Consultancy Management Standard (CMS)
rubrics_metrics.description: PRCA member organizations (not individual practitioners) must attain and maintain Consultancy Management Standard (CMS) accreditation, undergoing formal review on eight criteria every two years; members must follow specific guidelines for dealing with media, clients, and competitors and enforce the Professional Charter and Codes of Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider membership/accreditation (e.g., PRCA CMS) as evidence of a consultancy's adherence to professional standards and codes of conduct when selecting a firm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to ICCO charters and international standards
rubrics_metrics.description: ICCO promotes standards of professional practice (The Stockholm Charter), guidelines for media relations (Charter on Media Transparency), and adoption of quality accreditation (CMS) to raise standards, address ethical issues, standardize practice, and share knowledge among national associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate firms' membership in or adherence to ICCO/PRCA charters as part of ethical and quality assessment, especially for international or cross-border work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose specialist firms for niche or technical needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Although many firms claim to be 'full-service,' some carve out specialized client–service market niches (e.g., government relations, investor relations, health care, high tech, sports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select firms with demonstrated specialty experience for domain-specific communications (e.g., investor relations requires different skills than consumer PR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals who represent foreign interests must register with the U.S. Department of Justice as required under FARA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When hiring or representing foreign governments or interests, ensure legal compliance (registration) to avoid regulatory risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason to retain outside counsel: lack of prior PR program/experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Management has not previously conducted a formal public relations program and lacks experience in organizing one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hire outside counsel when internal expertise or experience in organizing PR programs is missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason to retain outside counsel: geographic distance from communications centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Headquarters may be located far from communications and financial centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain outside firms with proximity or networks in key media/financial centers when headquarters are remote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason to retain outside counsel: firm has wide range of up-to-date contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The firm has a wide range of up-to-date contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer firms with demonstrable, current media, analyst, policymaker, and stakeholder contacts relevant to your objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason to retain outside counsel: access to experienced executives and creative specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: An outside firm can provide the services of experienced executives and creative specialists who would be unwilling to move to other cities or whose salaries a single organization could not afford.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use outside counsel to access specialized talent or senior expertise that an organization cannot or will not hire full-time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason to retain outside counsel: need for highly specialized, non-continuous services
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization with its own PR department may need highly specialized services that it cannot afford or does not need on a full-time, continuous basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage firms for episodic specialized needs (e.g., major campaign, litigation communications, investor roadshows) rather than staffing permanently for low-frequency requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason to retain outside counsel: need for independent judgment on crucial policy matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Crucial policy matters require the independent judgment of an outsider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring in external counsel when impartial, independent advice is required to navigate sensitive policy or reputational issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public relations audit as the initial exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: The counsel begins by researching the client’s problem situation and its relationships with the publics affected by or involved in the situation; called a 'public relations audit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require a documented audit at the proposal stage to ensure the firm understands situation, stakeholders, and baseline metrics before work begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: New business pitch criterion: research findings and situation analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation should include research findings and situation analysis of the problem or opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate pitches on the quality and relevance of research and the depth of situation analysis presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: New business pitch criterion: threats and gains given various courses of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation should outline threats and gains to the organization, given various courses of action or nonaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the firm's strategic thinking by how well it articulates risks and benefits of alternative approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: New business pitch criterion: immediate action and communication responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation should specify immediate action and communication responses, if needed to meet a crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inquire whether the firm has actionable crisis response plans and rapid-response capabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: New business pitch criterion: overall strategy and program goals and objectives for various publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation should present overall strategy and program goals, as well as objectives for various publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge proposals by how clearly they link strategy to measurable objectives for each key public.

rubrics_metrics.name: New business pitch criterion: highlights of the communication and action program for achieving goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation should include highlights of the communication and action program for achieving the goals and objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for concrete program components and tactical sequencing that align with stated goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: New business pitch criterion: evaluation research plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation should include an evaluation research plan for monitoring the program and assessing impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear evaluation methods and KPIs up front to measure program performance and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: New business pitch criterion: staffing, budget, and timetable
rubrics_metrics.description: Presentation should outline staffing, budget, and timetable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize proposed team members, realistic budgets, and timelines to judge deliverability and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counselor engagement modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Once retained, the counselor usually functions in one of three ways: (1) provides advice and strategic plan, leaving execution to the client's internal staff; (2) provides advice and works with the client's staff to execute the program; (3) provides advice and undertakes full execution of the program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify the expected mode of engagement in the contract and evaluate firms on their demonstrated ability in the chosen mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bait-and-switch anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Some firms present a senior, experienced team during the new-business pitch but assign junior staff to do the work after winning the account; critics call this 'bait-and-switch.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require contractual commitments or staffing guarantees to prevent bait-and-switch; monitor actual staff participation and hold firms accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative RFP pitches and ethical limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Some clients solicit proposals to obtain new ideas without intention to pay; some firms refuse speculative pitches unless the client signs an agreement preventing use of ideas or pays a fee to cover preparation costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect intellectual property in RFPs: require compensation or non-use agreements for speculative creative work; consider paying for pitch development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of outside counsel: flexibility of talents and skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Counseling firms emphasize a variety of personnel and operations available to reinforce and upgrade a client's internal staff (researchers, artists, media specialists, media coaches, photographers, videographers, legislative experts, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose firms that demonstrate depth and breadth of specialist resources that can be mobilized quickly for diverse needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of outside counsel: objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity, relatively untrammeled by internal politics, is a major advantage; organizations often seek outsiders' perspectives free of history and power bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external counsel when unbiased assessment and candor are required to break internal deadlocks or surface difficult truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of outside counsel: range of prior experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms accumulate 'living case histories' across clients and problems, bringing lessons from prior successes and failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prospective firms on demonstrated track records with similar problems and on lessons learned applied to your context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of outside counsel: geographical scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms can provide geographic reach (national and global networks) that an internal department may lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-region or international needs, prefer firms with relevant local offices, affiliates, or network partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of outside counsel: reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: A counselor's reputation among press and officials can work to the client's advantage and top management may pay more attention when a reputable firm is engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reputation and public standing as factors that can open doors or lend credibility during high-profile matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantage: internal opposition to outside counsel
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal opposition ranges from nonacceptance to outright rejection; the 'old guard' may resist new ideas and see outsiders as threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare change-management and stakeholder-engagement plans to mitigate internal resistance when introducing external counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantage: cost and hours billed as frequent client complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of cost and hours billed are the most common threats to client–firm relationships; clients may perceive monthly invoices with hourly rates as excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide transparent fee structures, detailed time logs, and clear value explanations to reduce billing disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantage: conflicts of personality or conviction ('chemistry')
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts of personality or conviction occur; many clients cite 'good chemistry' as a key criterion when selecting a new firm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess interpersonal fit and working style during selection; include trial engagements or chemistry meetings as part of the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantage: distance and availability problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulties caused by distance and availability contribute to friction; clients expect full attention and prompt response despite firms serving many clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set service-level expectations, designate on-call contacts, and require responsiveness clauses in agreements to address availability concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantage: clients' lack of understanding and unavailability for approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: Clients' lack of understanding of PR and unavailability of client management for approvals can impede progress; client inattention may be a symptom of needing outside counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish clear approval processes, governance, and client responsibilities upfront to prevent delays and misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Billing methods for counseling firms
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees are typically established in one of four ways: (1) monthly retainer covering fixed/flexible hours and services; (2) minimum monthly retainer plus billing for actual staff time above retainer; (3) straight hourly charges for staff time; (4) fixed project fee, typically from competitive bidding in response to an RFP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a billing method that aligns incentives and project scope; clarify what services/outputs are covered by retainers or fixed fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment-by-results is misleading (criticized fifth billing approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some firms offer 'payment-by-results' but measure 'results' as media coverage, website hits, or contacts—indicators of effort rather than ultimate impact (behaviour change, response to call to action, reputation value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of 'pay-for-coverage' models; define meaningful outcome metrics (behavior change, sales lift, reputation indicators) rather than proxy media metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements reflected in counseling fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Five elements reflected in counseling fees: (1) actual cost of staff time; (2) executive time and supervision; (3) administrative and other nonproject time; (4) overhead costs (space, benefits, utilities); (5) reasonable profit based on market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating fees, ask firms to break down charges across these elements to understand cost drivers and judge fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed project fees risk loss of continuity and uncoordinated tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: The trend toward fixed project fees can change the nature of business; firms may have to compete for many small projects, leading to loss of continuity and an uncoordinated series of tactics that are not part of an overall strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance project-based contracts with provisions for strategic oversight and continuity (e.g., strategic retainer, coordination fees, or program-level contracts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Out-of-pocket expenses billing and markups
rubrics_metrics.description: Out-of-pocket expenses are generally billed at cost and exclusive of the retainer fee; some firms mark up actual costs of certain expenses by 15–20 percent to cover overhead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify expense billing terms and allowed markups in the contract; require supporting invoices for reimbursable expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical fee ranges and profitability benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Counseling firms have minimum retainer fees usually $1,000–$10,000 (up to $100,000+ for major accounts); hourly fees range from ~$60 for junior staff to several hundred dollars for senior counselors; firms target ~25% pretax profit and revenue per professional varies by firm size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use market benchmarks to evaluate proposed fees and assess firm financial health, but prioritize value and fit over lowest cost alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Billable hours as a productivity and evaluation metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Some firms expect each practitioner to 'bill out' a minimum of 30 hours each week; employees record time in tenths or quarter-hours and client invoices reflect total hours charged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand firm expectations around billable hours; for long-term engagements, include time reporting transparency and productivity metrics in the agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: New approaches: mix of internal and external counsel; keep core PR in-house
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations increasingly use a combination of internal departments and outside counsel. Predictions include smaller, tight, expert internal PR departments and increased outsourcing; however, high-priority, core responsibilities should remain in-house.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain core strategic PR functions internally (strategy, senior counsel) and outsource specialized or noncritical activities to firms, while ensuring integration and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective disclosure and legal/ethical limits on communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating in the public gaze does not mean everything should be made public—there are competitors, security, ethical, patient-privacy, political, and regulatory considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define disclosure policies with legal counsel and PR to balance transparency with confidentiality, compliance, and strategic considerations.
